# Java Revision — Interview & Concept Guide
### Topics from Step 2 Code Only

---

## 1. Records (Java 16 — GA)

### What it is
A `record` is a restricted class that is immutable by default.
The compiler auto-generates: canonical constructor, component getters,
`equals()`, `hashCode()`, and `toString()`.

### Used in this project
`Patient.java`, `PatientResponse.java`, `ReferralResponse.java`,
`ErrorResponse.java`, `PatientStatus` inner types (Admitted, Outpatient, etc.)

### Syntax
```java
public record Patient(String id, String name, int age) { }

// Auto-generated by compiler — you don't write these:
// public Patient(String id, String name, int age) { ... }
// public String id() { return id; }
// public boolean equals(Object o) { ... }
// public int hashCode() { ... }
// public String toString() { ... }
```

### Compact constructor (validation)
```java
public record Patient(String id, String name, int age) {
    public Patient {                        // no parameter list — compact form
        if (id == null || id.isBlank())
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("id must not be blank");
    }
}
```

### Key rules for interviews
- Records are implicitly `final` — cannot be extended
- All components are `private final` — immutable
- Records CAN implement interfaces (used for PatientStatus inner records)
- Records CANNOT extend classes (implicitly extend `java.lang.Record`)
- Getters use component name, not `getX()` — `patient.id()` not `patient.getId()`

### Java 8 equivalent
```java
// Java 8 — requires Lombok @Value or ~40 lines of boilerplate
@Value  // Lombok
public class Patient {
    String id;
    String name;
    int age;
}
```

## 2. Sealed Interfaces (Java 17 — GA)

### What it is
A sealed interface restricts which classes can implement it.
Only types listed in `permits` are valid subtypes.
Makes the type hierarchy **closed** and **exhaustive**.

### Used in this project
`PatientStatus.java`, `ReferralStatus.java`

### Syntax
```java
public sealed interface PatientStatus
        permits PatientStatus.Admitted,
                PatientStatus.Outpatient,
                PatientStatus.Critical,
                PatientStatus.Discharged {

    String value();
    boolean isActive();
}

// Each permitted type — using records for zero boilerplate
record Admitted() implements PatientStatus {
    public String  value()    { return "admitted"; }
    public boolean isActive() { return true;       }
}
```

### Why sealed over enum?
```java
// Enum approach — isActive() needs a switch internally
enum PatientStatus {
    ADMITTED, OUTPATIENT, CRITICAL, DISCHARGED;

    public boolean isActive() {
        return switch (this) {
            case ADMITTED, OUTPATIENT, CRITICAL -> true;
            case DISCHARGED -> false;
        };
    }
}

// Sealed approach — each variant OWNS its behaviour, no switch needed
record Admitted() implements PatientStatus {
    public boolean isActive() { return true; }  // self-contained
}
```

### Key rules for interviews
- `sealed` classes/interfaces must be in the same package or module as `permits` types
- Permitted subtypes must be `final`, `sealed`, or `non-sealed`
- Records are implicitly final — perfect match for sealed permits
- The compiler can verify exhaustiveness in switch expressions

## 3. Switch Expressions (Java 14 — GA)

### What it is
Switch that **returns a value** directly using `->` arrow cases.
No fall-through, no `break` needed.

### Used in this project
`PatientStatus.from()`, `ReferralStatus.from()`

### Syntax comparison
```java
// Java 8 — switch STATEMENT (no return value, needs break)
String label;
switch (raw.toLowerCase()) {
    case "admitted":
        label = "ADMITTED";
        break;
    case "discharged":
        label = "DISCHARGED";
        break;
    default:
        throw new IllegalArgumentException("Unknown: " + raw);
}

// Java 14+ — switch EXPRESSION (returns value, no break)
PatientStatus status = switch (raw.toLowerCase()) {
    case "admitted"   -> new Admitted();
    case "discharged" -> new Discharged();
    default -> throw new IllegalArgumentException("Unknown: " + raw);
};
```

### Key rules for interviews
- Arrow cases (`->`) do not fall through — no break needed
- Switch expression must be exhaustive (all cases covered or default present)
- Can use `yield` keyword to return from a block case
- Works with: String, int, enum, and with sealed types (Java 21 full pattern matching)

## 4. Pattern Matching instanceof (Java 16 — GA)

### What it is
Combines the `instanceof` check and the cast into one step.
Eliminates the redundant explicit cast.

### Used in this project
Conceptually in `PatientService.describeStatus()` — shows the pattern.

### Syntax comparison
```java
// Java 8 — explicit cast after instanceof check
Object obj = getPatient();
if (obj instanceof Patient) {
    Patient p = (Patient) obj;   // redundant cast
    System.out.println(p.name());
}

// Java 16+ — pattern variable declared inline
if (obj instanceof Patient p) {
    System.out.println(p.name()); // p is already Patient type here
}
```

---

## 5. Stream.toList() (Java 16)

### What it is
Terminal stream operation that returns an **unmodifiable** `List`.
Replaces the verbose `collect(Collectors.toUnmodifiableList())`.

### Used in this project
Every service method: `getAllPatients()`, `getPatientsByStatus()`, etc.

### Comparison
```java
// Java 8
List<PatientResponse> result = patients.stream()
    .map(PatientResponse::from)
    .collect(Collectors.toList());         // mutable list

// Java 10+
List<PatientResponse> result = patients.stream()
    .map(PatientResponse::from)
    .collect(Collectors.toUnmodifiableList()); // immutable list

// Java 16+
List<PatientResponse> result = patients.stream()
    .map(PatientResponse::from)
    .toList();                             // immutable list — cleanest form
```

### Interview note
`Stream.toList()` returns an **unmodifiable** list (like `List.of()`).
`Collectors.toList()` returns a **mutable** list.
This is a subtle but interview-worthy distinction.

---

## 6. List.of() and Map.of() (Java 9)

### What it is
Factory methods that create **unmodifiable** collections in one line.

### Used in this project
`PatientService` in-memory store, `PatientController.health()` response

### Syntax
```java
// Java 8
List<String> list = new ArrayList<>();
list.add("a"); list.add("b");
list = Collections.unmodifiableList(list);

// Java 9+
List<String> list = List.of("a", "b");         // unmodifiable, null-safe

Map<String, String> map = Map.of(
    "status",  "UP",
    "service", "patient-service"
);
```

### Key rules for interviews
- `List.of()` does NOT allow null elements — throws `NullPointerException`
- `List.of()` is unordered for sets, ordered for lists
- Max 10 key-value pairs for `Map.of()` — use `Map.ofEntries()` for more
- Any mutating call (`.add()`, `.put()`, `.remove()`) throws `UnsupportedOperationException`

---

## 7. Optional and orElseThrow() (Java 8+)

### What it is
A container that may or may not hold a value.
Forces you to handle the "not present" case explicitly.

### Used in this project
`PatientService.getPatientById()`, `ReferralService.getReferralById()`

### Syntax
```java
// Java 8 — anti-pattern: calling get() without check
Optional<Patient> opt = findById(id);
Patient p = opt.get();   // throws NoSuchElementException if empty — bad!

// Java 8 — correct: orElseThrow with lambda
Patient p = patients.stream()
    .filter(pat -> pat.id().equals(id))
    .findFirst()
    .orElseThrow(() -> new PatientNotFoundException(id));
```

### Key rules for interviews
- Never call `Optional.get()` without `isPresent()` — it's the null check you were trying to avoid
- `orElseThrow(Supplier)` is preferred over `orElseThrow()` (no-arg throws `NoSuchElementException`)
- `Optional` should NOT be used as a field type or method parameter — only as return type
- `Optional.map()` and `Optional.flatMap()` allow chained transformations

---

## 8. Method References (Java 8)

### What it is
A shorthand for a lambda that calls a single existing method.

### Used in this project
`.map(PatientResponse::from)` in every service method

### Types of method references
```java
// Static method reference
.map(PatientResponse::from)
// equivalent lambda: .map(p -> PatientResponse.from(p))

// Instance method reference on a specific object
list.forEach(System.out::println)
// equivalent lambda: list.forEach(s -> System.out.println(s))

// Instance method reference on arbitrary object of a type
.filter(String::isBlank)
// equivalent lambda: .filter(s -> s.isBlank())

// Constructor reference
.map(Patient::new)
// equivalent lambda: .map(args -> new Patient(args))
```

---

## Java 8 → 17 Feature Timeline (Quick Reference)

| Version | Feature |
|---------|---------|
| Java 8  | Streams, Lambdas, Optional, Method refs, Default methods |
| Java 9  | `List.of()`, `Map.of()`, `Set.of()`, modules |
| Java 10 | `var` keyword (local variable type inference) |
| Java 11 | `String.isBlank()`, `String.strip()`, `Files.readString()` |
| Java 14 | Switch expressions (GA) |
| Java 15 | Text blocks (GA) |
| Java 16 | Records (GA), Pattern matching instanceof (GA), `Stream.toList()` |
| Java 17 | Sealed interfaces (GA) — LTS release |

## Common Interview Questions on These Topics

**Q: What is the difference between a record and a class?**
A: Records are immutable, final, auto-generate boilerplate, and use component accessors (no getX pattern). Classes are mutable by default, extendable, and require explicit method declarations.

**Q: Why use sealed interfaces instead of enums?**
A: Sealed types allow each variant to be its own full class/record with its own fields and behaviour. Enums are limited to constant values. Sealed types enable exhaustive pattern matching and richer domain modelling.

**Q: What does Stream.toList() return vs Collectors.toList()?**
A: `Stream.toList()` returns an unmodifiable list (Java 16+). `Collectors.toList()` returns a mutable list. Using `toList()` enforces immutability which is safer in concurrent or stateless service code.

**Q: Why is Optional.get() considered bad practice?**
A: It throws `NoSuchElementException` if the Optional is empty — the same problem as NullPointerException but with less context. Always use `orElseThrow()`, `orElse()`, or `orElseGet()`.



# Java Revision — Interview & Concept Guide
### Step 4: JWT Auth (New Java concepts introduced)

## 1. ThreadLocal<T> — per-thread isolated storage

### What it is
`ThreadLocal<T>` provides a variable where each thread has its own independent value.
No synchronisation is needed — threads can never see each other's values.

### Used in this project
`UserContextHolder.java` — stores `UserContext` per request thread.

### Syntax comparison
```java
// Java 8 — ThreadLocal declaration
private static final ThreadLocal<UserContext> HOLDER = new ThreadLocal<>();

// Java 17 — identical syntax (ThreadLocal hasn't changed)
// but the stored TYPE (UserContext) is now a record — immutable
private static final ThreadLocal<UserContext> HOLDER = new ThreadLocal<>();
```

### How it works in Tomcat
```
Thread 1 (Request from Dr. Mehta):
  HOLDER.set(new UserContext("U001", "dr.mehta@trucare.com", "DOCTOR", "Dr. Mehta"))
  Controller reads HOLDER.get() → UserContext{userId=U001, role=DOCTOR}
  HOLDER.remove()   ← CRITICAL cleanup

Thread 2 (Request from Nurse Priya — same time):
  HOLDER.set(new UserContext("U002", "priya@trucare.com", "NURSE", "Nurse Priya"))
  Controller reads HOLDER.get() → UserContext{userId=U002, role=NURSE}
  HOLDER.remove()   ← each thread cleans its own slot
```

Thread 1 and Thread 2 never see each other's UserContext.

### The memory leak trap
```java
// WRONG — causes memory leak in thread-pool environments
HOLDER.set(null);      // sets null but thread-local slot still exists

// CORRECT — fully removes the thread-local binding
HOLDER.remove();       // frees the memory completely
```

Tomcat reuses threads from its pool. If Thread 1 doesn't call `.remove()`,
the next request on Thread 1 sees the previous user's context.
This is a security bug AND a memory leak.

### Interview note
> "ThreadLocal is one of the most misused Java concurrency tools. Its correct use is
> for per-request context in thread-per-request frameworks like Tomcat. The critical rule
> is always calling `.remove()` in a finally block or interceptor `afterCompletion()`.
> Spring's own `RequestContextHolder`, `SecurityContextHolder`, and `TransactionSynchronizationManager`
> all use ThreadLocal internally."

---

## 2. HandlerInterceptor — Spring MVC request lifecycle hook

### What it is
An interface with three lifecycle methods that wrap every controller invocation.

### Used in this project
`JwtClaimsInterceptor.java`

### Three hook points
```java
public interface HandlerInterceptor {

    // Runs BEFORE controller — return false to abort request
    default boolean preHandle(HttpServletRequest req,
                              HttpServletResponse res,
                              Object handler) throws Exception {
        return true;
    }

    // Runs AFTER controller, BEFORE response written
    // Can modify ModelAndView — rarely used in REST APIs
    default void postHandle(HttpServletRequest req,
                            HttpServletResponse res,
                            Object handler,
                            ModelAndView mv) throws Exception { }

    // Runs AFTER response written — use for cleanup
    default void afterCompletion(HttpServletRequest req,
                                 HttpServletResponse res,
                                 Object handler,
                                 Exception ex) throws Exception { }
}
```

### Java 8 default methods — why no abstract class needed
Before Java 8, Spring provided `HandlerInterceptorAdapter` (abstract class)
so you only had to implement the methods you needed.
After Java 8, interface default methods made the adapter redundant.
`HandlerInterceptorAdapter` was deprecated in Spring 5.3.

```java
// Java 7 era — had to extend adapter to avoid implementing all 3 methods
public class JwtInterceptor extends HandlerInterceptorAdapter {
    @Override
    public boolean preHandle(...) { ... }
    // postHandle and afterCompletion inherited as no-ops from adapter
}

// Java 8+ — implement interface directly, use defaults for unused methods
public class JwtInterceptor implements HandlerInterceptor {
    @Override
    public boolean preHandle(...) { ... }
    // postHandle and afterCompletion use interface default implementations
}
```

## 3. Record compact constructor — validation pattern

### Used in this project
`UserContext.java` compact constructor validates `userId` is present.

```java
public record UserContext(String userId, String email,
                          String role, String name) {
    // Compact constructor — parameters already assigned when this runs
    public UserContext {
        if (userId == null || userId.isBlank()) {
            throw new IllegalStateException(
                "X-User-Id header missing — check KrakenD config");
        }
    }
}
```

### Why `IllegalStateException` not `IllegalArgumentException`
```
IllegalArgumentException → caller passed a bad argument (their fault)
IllegalStateException    → system is in an unexpected state (our config fault)
```

Missing `X-User-Id` means KrakenD didn't propagate the claim — that's a
configuration error in `krakend.json`, not bad user input.
The exception type communicates who is at fault.

---

## 4. Static factory methods on records

### Used in this project
`UserContext.anonymous()` — creates a GUEST context for public endpoints.

```java
public record UserContext(String userId, String email,
                          String role, String name) {

    // Static factory — named constructor communicates intent
    public static UserContext anonymous() {
        return new UserContext("anonymous", null, "GUEST", null);
    }
}
```

### Java 8 equivalent
```java
// Java 8 — static factory on a regular class
public class UserContext {
    public static UserContext anonymous() {
        return new UserContext("anonymous", null, "GUEST", null);
    }
}
```

### Why named factory over constructor
`new UserContext("anonymous", null, "GUEST", null)` — unclear, error-prone
`UserContext.anonymous()` — self-documenting, impossible to pass args in wrong order

---

## 5. Logger and SLF4J — production logging pattern

### Used in this project
`PatientController`, `ReferralController`, `JwtClaimsInterceptor` all use SLF4J.

```java
// Java 17 — field declaration
private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(PatientController.class);

// Usage — parameterised to avoid string concatenation when logging is disabled
log.info("GET /patients/{} accessed by userId={} role={}", id, ctx.userId(), ctx.role());
```

### Why parameterised logging matters
```java
// WRONG — string concatenated even when INFO logging is disabled
log.info("GET /patients/" + id + " by " + ctx.userId() + " role=" + ctx.role());

// CORRECT — {} placeholders only evaluated if INFO is enabled
log.info("GET /patients/{} by userId={} role={}", id, ctx.userId(), ctx.role());
```

At DEBUG level in production (logging.level.com.trucare=WARN), the parameterised
version creates zero string objects. The WRONG version creates strings even when
the log line is discarded — wasted GC pressure on every request.

### Log levels — when to use each
| Level | Use for |
|---|---|
| `ERROR` | System failures, exceptions that need immediate attention |
| `WARN` | Unexpected but recoverable situations |
| `INFO` | Business events — who did what (audit trail) |
| `DEBUG` | Developer diagnostics — request/response details |
| `TRACE` | Fine-grained flow — rarely used in production |

## Common Interview Questions from Step 4

**Q: What is ThreadLocal and when should you use it?**

A: ThreadLocal provides per-thread storage — each thread gets its own isolated
copy of the value with no synchronisation needed. Use it for per-request context
in thread-per-request servers like Tomcat, where you need to pass contextual data
(user identity, request ID, locale) through call chains without modifying method
signatures. The critical rule: always call `.remove()` in cleanup code —
Tomcat reuses threads and leaked ThreadLocal values corrupt subsequent requests.

**Q: What is the difference between `HandlerInterceptor` and a Servlet `Filter`?**

A: A Servlet Filter operates at the Servlet container level — it sees the raw
`HttpServletRequest` before Spring MVC processes it, and runs for ALL requests
including static resources. A `HandlerInterceptor` operates inside Spring MVC —
it runs only for requests handled by `@Controller` methods, has access to the
handler object, and integrates with Spring's exception handling.
For cross-cutting concerns like user context population, `HandlerInterceptor`
is preferred because it participates in the Spring MVC lifecycle.

**Q: Why use `IllegalStateException` instead of `IllegalArgumentException`?**

A: `IllegalArgumentException` signals the caller passed invalid data — it's their
fault. `IllegalStateException` signals the system is in an inconsistent state —
it's a configuration or programming error. Missing `X-User-Id` in our code means
KrakenD didn't propagate the claim correctly — that's our configuration problem,
not bad user input, so `IllegalStateException` is semantically correct.
